Multiplicative and Additive Finite Free Convolution For qq-Polynomials

Andrei Martínez-Finkelshtein AMFDepartment of Mathematics, Baylor University, TX, USA, and Department of Mathematics, University of Almería, Spain Email address: a_martinez-finkelshtein@baylor.edu , Rafael Morales RMDepartment of Mathematics, Baylor University, TX, USA Email address: rafael_morales2@baylor.edu and Daniel Perales DPDepartment of Mathematics, University of Notre Dame, IN, USA Email address: dperale2@nd.edu
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We study qq-analogs of finite free convolutions and their interaction with families of qq-hypergeometric polynomials. First, we revisit the qq-multiplicative finite free convolution, previously introduced in the literature, and show that it acts naturally on qq-hypergeometric polynomials: the convolution of two such polynomials remains within the same class, with parameters obtained by concatenation. This observation provides a simple mechanism for constructing large families of qq-hypergeometric polynomials whose zeros are real and whose logarithmic mesh is controlled. We illustrate it with an example of multiple little qq-Jacobi polynomials of the first kind. A result of independent interest is also an alternative definition of the qq-multiplicative convolution in terms of qq-differential operators.

Motivated by the additive finite free convolution, we introduce a qq-additive finite free convolution and study its algebraic and analytic properties. Although this convolution does not preserve real-rootedness in general, we show that a natural modification involving a qq-multiplicative convolution restores the preservation of real roots and interlacing for polynomials with bounded logarithmic mesh.

Finally, we develop a systematic method to translate product identities of qq-hypergeometric functions into convolution identities for qq-hypergeometric polynomials. This approach yields several explicit formulas for qq-additive convolutions and produces new families of real-rooted qq-hypergeometric polynomials.

Key words and phrases:
qq-hypergeometric polynomials; Finite free convolution; Free probability; Zeros

1. Introduction

Finite free convolution operations have become an important tool in the study of real-rooted polynomials and spectral phenomena. They were introduced in the work of Marcus, Spielman, and Srivastava [MSS22] as part of their resolution of the Kadison–Singer problem. These operations provide algebraic transformations of polynomials that preserve real-rootedness and interlacing properties, and have since found applications in spectral graph theory, random matrix theory, and the theory of hyperbolic polynomials. Closely related ideas had appeared earlier in the classical work of Walsh [Wal50] and Szegő [PS14, Sze22] (see also [KS06]), who studied transformations preserving the location and interlacing of zeros of real polynomials.

Two fundamental operations in this context are the additive and multiplicative finite free convolutions. Both can be defined explicitly in terms of the coefficients of polynomials and have strong stability properties with respect to real zeros. In particular, the additive finite free convolution preserves real-rootedness and interlacing, while the multiplicative convolution preserves real-rootedness for polynomials whose zeros lie in suitable half-lines. These results provide a powerful algebraic framework for constructing new families of real-rooted polynomials from known ones, which was successfully exploited in [MFMP24] in the framework of hypergeometric polynomials. Finite free convolution turned out to be a tool that allows us to derive conclusions about the zeros of these polynomials from the corresponding properties of more elementary “building blocks.”

The main goal of this paper is to extend this machinery to the qq-hypergeometric polynomials. The theory of basic hypergeometric series has long provided a rich source of special functions and orthogonal polynomials families. Truncations of basic hypergeometric series lead to the so-called qq-hypergeometric polynomials; see, for instance, [KLS10]. The location and interlacing properties of the zeros of these polynomials have been investigated in a variety of settings; see, e.g., [GJRS16b, Moa81]. These results reveal a remarkable dependence of the zero distribution on the parameters of the hypergeometric series and show that many such polynomials have entirely real zeros under explicit parameter conditions.

However, the finite free convolutions, used as in [MFMP24], do not preserve the main properties of qq-hypergeometric polynomials, and have to be adapted to this context. The first modification of this type of binary operations on polynomials, known as the qq-multiplicative finite free convolution and denoted by ⊠n,q\boxtimes_{n,q}, was introduced by Lamprecht [Lam16] and can be viewed as a deformation of the standard multiplicative finite convolution appearing in free probability.

We show that this operation interacts remarkably well with qq-hypergeometric polynomials. The starting point is the observation that the qq-multiplicative convolution of two qq-hypergeometric polynomials is again a qq-hypergeometric polynomial whose parameters are obtained by concatenation of the parameter sets of the factors. This is a qq-analog of the hypergeometric convolution structure observed in [MFMP24]. It provides a simple and systematic mechanism for constructing large families of qq-hypergeometric polynomials with controlled zero distribution. In particular, by combining this operation with known real-rooted qq-hypergeometric families, we obtain broad classes of polynomials whose zeros are real and whose relative spacing (or logarithmic mesh) is bounded. Moreover, we derive a simple equivalent definition of the qq-multiplicative finite convolution in terms of some qq-differential operators, an apparently new result that has an independent interest.

In the second part of the paper, we introduce a qq-analog of the additive finite free convolution, that is, a binary operation ⊞n,q\boxplus_{n,q} acting on polynomials of degree at most nn. It is defined in terms of the coefficients of the polynomial factors, but as in the previous case, it admits a natural representation in terms of qq-differential operators and can therefore be connected directly with the analytic structure of basic hypergeometric series. It allows us to develop a systematic method to rewrite factorization formulas for qq-hypergeometric functions as identities involving qq-additive convolutions of qq-hypergeometric polynomials (again, as a qq-analog of the similar identities developed in [MFMP24]). As illustrations, we derive several explicit formulas for qq-additive convolutions of qq-hypergeometric polynomials based on the classical product formulas such as Heine’s transformation and related identities for basic hypergeometric series.

The results of this paper provide new tools for constructing and analyzing real-rooted families of qq-hypergeometric polynomials. The qq-multiplicative finite free convolution ⊠n,q\boxtimes_{n,q} fits especially well with the qq-hypergeometric structure: the convolution of two qq-hypergeometric polynomials is again qq-hypergeometric, with parameters obtained by concatenation. Combined with known real-rootedness and interlacing criteria for basic hypergeometric polynomials, this gives a systematic way to generate new families with controlled zero location and logarithmic mesh.

The qq-additive convolution ⊞n,q\boxplus_{n,q}, introduced here as a qq-deformation of the additive finite free convolution, exhibits a different phenomenon. In contrast with the classical operation, ⊞n,q\boxplus_{n,q} does not preserve real-rootedness in general. Our main result in this direction is that this obstruction is removed by a universal qq-multiplicative correction. Namely, convolution with the fixed polynomial

ϕ11​(q−n0,q,−x),{}_{1}\phi_{1}\!\left(\begin{matrix}q^{-n}\\ 0\end{matrix};q,-x\right),

through ⊠n,q\boxtimes_{n,q}, restores real-rootedness for inputs in ℙnq​(ℝ)\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q}(\mathbb{R}). In the positive case p,r∈ℙnq​(ℝ>0)p,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}), the corrected polynomial also has positive zeros and satisfies the same logarithmic-mesh bound. We further obtain an analogous preservation result for interlacing. In this sense, the corrected qq-additive convolution recovers, under natural logarithmic-mesh hypotheses, the zero-preserving behavior characteristic of the classical additive finite free convolution.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review basic notions concerning real-rooted polynomials, interlacing, logarithmic mesh, and qq-hypergeometric polynomials. Section 3 studies the qq-multiplicative finite free convolution and its action on qq-hypergeometric polynomials, including the parameter concatenation phenomenon described above. In Section 4, we introduce the qq-additive finite free convolution, analyze its algebraic properties, and establish real roots preservation, as explained above. Finally, Section 5 develops a general method for translating product identities of basic hypergeometric functions into convolution identities for qq-hypergeometric polynomials and presents several illustrative examples. Some technical proofs are deferred to Appendices A and B.

p∈ℙnq​(ℝ>0)⇒𝔡q​p∈ℙn−1q​(ℝ>0)​ and ​p≺𝔡q​p.p\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathfrak{d}_{q}p\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})\text{ and }p\prec\mathfrak{d}_{q}p.

Proposition 2.4.

Let pp be a polynomial of degree nn with simple positive roots. Then

𝔡q​p∈ℙn−1​(ℝ>0)​ and ​p≺𝔡q​p⇒lmeshp<q.\mathfrak{d}_{q}p\in\mathbb{P}_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})\text{ and }p\prec\mathfrak{d}_{q}p\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathop{\rm lmesh}p<q.
Proof.

By hypothesis p≺𝔡q​pp\prec\mathfrak{d}_{q}p and from the definition of 𝔡q\mathfrak{d}_{q} we know that

p⁡(q​x)=p⁡(x)−x​𝔡q​p​(x).p(qx)=p(x)-x\mathfrak{d}_{q}p(x).

By Lemma 2.2, we get that either p⁡(x)≺p⁡(q​x)p(x)\prec p(qx) or p⁡(q​x)≺p⁡(x)p(qx)\prec p(x). Since pp has positive roots then p⁡(x)≺p⁡(q​x)p(x)\prec p(qx), which is equivalent to p∈ℙnq​(ℝ>0)p\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}) by (4). ∎

Remark 2.5.

Note that Proposition 2.4 still holds if we replace the hypothesis of p≺𝔡q​pp\prec\mathfrak{d}_{q}p by p≺(𝔡q​p)​(q−1​x)p\prec(\mathfrak{d}_{q}p)(q^{-1}x). The proof is completely analogous, but using

p⁡(q​x)=p⁡(x)+x⁡(𝔡q​p)​(q−1​x).p(qx)=p(x)+x(\mathfrak{d}_{q}p)(q^{-1}x).

3. qq-Multiplicative Convolution

3.1. Preliminary results

In this section, we will introduce definitions and results of qq-multiplicative convolution, studied in [Lam16].

In what follows, we will denote the coefficients of a polynomial pp of degree nn as follows:

(18) p⁡(x)=∑j=0nxn−j​ej​(p).p(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}x^{n-j}e_{j}(p).

Since we do not require a priori e0​(p)≠0e_{0}(p)\neq 0, the notation ej​(p)e_{j}(p) implicitly assumes the dependence on nn. It is convenient to keep it in mind, since we will avoid mentioning it explicitly to simplify the notation.

Definition 3.1.

Given two polynomials, pp and rr, of degree at most nn, the nn-th qq-multiplicative finite free convolution of pp and rr, denoted by p⊠n,qrp\boxtimes_{n,q}r, is a polynomial of degree at most nn, which, following the notational convention (18), is defined as

[p⊠n,qr]​(x):=∑k=0nek​(p⊠n,qr)​xn−k,[p\boxtimes_{n,q}r](x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}e_{k}(p\boxtimes_{n,q}r)x^{n-k},

with

(19) ek​(p⊠n,qr)=(q,q)n−k(q−n,q)n−k​ek​(p)​ek​(r).e_{k}(p\boxtimes_{n,q}r)=\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n-k}}{\left(q^{-n};q\right)_{n-k}}\,e_{k}(p)e_{k}(r).

This definition differs from the given in [Lam16] only by a rescaling of xx by −q−n-q^{-n}. This is done to simplify the notation when applied to qq-hypergeometric polynomials.

The qq-multiplicative finite free convolution is a linear operator from ℙn×ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n}\times\mathbb{P}_{n} to ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n}: if p,r,g∈ℙnp,r,g\in\mathbb{P}_{n}, and α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}, then

(α​p+g)⊠n,qr=α⁡(p⊠n,qr)+g⊠n,qr.(\alpha p+g)\boxtimes_{n,q}r=\alpha(p\boxtimes_{n,q}r)+g\boxtimes_{n,q}r.

The identity for the qq-multiplicative convolution is given by the polynomial

(20) En,q(x):=∏k=1n(1−q−kx)=1ϕ0(.q−n⋅.;q,x),E_{n,q}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(1-q^{-k}x\right)={\ }_{1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{0}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n}}{\cdot};q,x\right)},

which has roots at q,q2,…​qnq,q^{2},\dots q^{n}. Indeed, one can check that ek​(En,q)=(q−n,q)n−k(q,q)n−ke_{k}\left(E_{n,q}\right)=\frac{\left(q^{-n};q\right)_{n-k}}{\left(q;q\right)_{n-k}} for k=0,…,nk=0,\dots,n, implying by Definition 3.1 that

(21) p\displaystyle p ⊠n,qEn,q=p for all p∈ℙn.\displaystyle\boxtimes_{n,q}E_{n,q}=p\qquad\text{ for all }p\in\mathbb{P}_{n}.

It can be easily checked that scaling of the variable in En,qE_{n,q} before its qq-multiplicative convolution has a simple effect on the result: for a scalar α\alpha,

(22) p⁡(x)⊠n,qEn,q​(α​x)=p⁡(α​x).p(x)\boxtimes_{n,q}E_{n,q}(\alpha x)=p\left(\alpha x\right).

As a consequence,

(23) p⁡(α​x)\displaystyle p(\alpha x) ⊠n,qr(βx)=p(x)⊠n,qr(αβx).\displaystyle\boxtimes_{n,q}r(\beta x)=p(x)\boxtimes_{n,q}r(\alpha\beta x).
Remark 3.2 (Relation with multiplicative finite free convolution).

Recall that for polynomials p,r∈ℙnp,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n} in the form (18), we define the nn-th multiplicative finite free convolution p⊠nrp\boxtimes_{n}r by

(24) ek(p⊠nr)=(−1)k(nk)−1ek(p)ek(r),k=0,1,…,n.e_{k}(p\boxtimes_{n}r)=(-1)^{k}\binom{n}{k}^{-1}e_{k}(p)e_{k}(r),\quad k=0,1,\dots,n.

It follows that

limq→1p⊠n,qr=p⊠nr.\lim_{q\to 1}p\boxtimes_{n,q}r=p\boxtimes_{n}r.

Indeed, using the limit property (6), one has

limq→1(q,q)n−k(q−n,q)n−k=limq→1(1−q)n−k​(q,q)n−k(q−n,q)n−k​(1−q)n−k=(−1)k​(nk)−1.\lim_{q\to 1}\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n-k}}{\left(q^{-n};q\right)_{n-k}}=\lim_{q\to 1}\frac{(1-q)^{n-k}\left(q;q\right)_{n-k}}{\left(q^{-n};q\right)_{n-k}(1-q)^{n-k}}=(-1)^{k}\binom{n}{k}^{-1}.

It turns out that the qq-multiplicative convolution can be computed in terms of qq-differential operators defined in (16), which can be taken as an alternative definition. This observation, to the best of our knowledge, is new.

With a polynomial p∈ℙnp\in\mathbb{P}_{n} we can associate its (x​𝔡q)(x\mathfrak{d}_{q})-dual polynomial pˇ∈ℙn\check{p}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}, such that

pˇ​(x​𝔡q)​[En,q​(x)]=p⁡(x).\check{p}(x\mathfrak{d}_{q})[E_{n,q}(x)]=p(x).

Indeed, pˇ\check{p} is the unique polynomial of degree nn such that

(25) pˇ(1−qk)=(q,q)k(q−n,q)kek(p),for k=0,1,…,n.\check{p}(1-q^{k})=\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{k}}{\left(q^{-n};q\right)_{k}}e_{k}(p),\qquad\text{for }k=0,1,\dots,n.

Following the ideas from [Mir21, Subsection 3.2.4], we obtain the following alternative definition of qq-multiplicative convolution.

Proposition 3.3.

Given polynomials p,r∈ℙnp,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}, let pˇ\check{p} and rˇ\check{r} be their (x​𝔡q)(x\mathfrak{d}_{q})-duals. Then

(p⊠n,qr)​(x)=pˇ​(x​𝔡q)​rˇ​(x​𝔡q)​[En,q​(x)].\left(p\boxtimes_{n,q}r\right)(x)=\check{p}(x\mathfrak{d}_{q})\check{r}(x\mathfrak{d}_{q})\left[E_{n,q}(x)\right].

As it was observed by [Lam16], the qq-multiplicative convolution preserves the real-rootedness of the polynomials under some additional assumptions. We reformulate them here, taking into account the rescaling by −q−n-q^{-n} in Definition 3.1 and the identity (23). Hence (see [Lam16, Theorem 3]):

Proposition 3.4.

Let p,r∈ℙnp,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}. Then

  1. (i)

    p∈ℙnq​(ℝ),r∈ℙnq​(ℝ>0)⇒p⊠n,qr∈ℙnq​(ℝ)p\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}),\ r\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})\ \Rightarrow\ p\boxtimes_{n,q}r\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}).

  2. (ii)

    p,r∈ℙnq​(ℝ>0)⇒p⊠n,qr∈ℙnq​(ℝ>0)p,r\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})\ \Rightarrow\ p\boxtimes_{n,q}r\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}).

Taking into account that p⁡(−x)=p⊠n,qEn,q​(−x)p(-x)=p\boxtimes_{n,q}E_{n,q}(-x) (see (22) with α=−1\alpha=-1), a simple consequence of this proposition is that additionally the following “rule of signs” applies:

  • •

    p,r∈ℙnq​(ℝ<0)⇒p⊠n,qr∈ℙnq​(ℝ>0)p,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q}(\mathbb{R}_{<0})\ \Rightarrow\ p\boxtimes_{n,q}r\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}),

  • •

    p∈ℙnq​(ℝ<0),r∈ℙnq​(ℝ>0)⇒p⊠n,qr∈ℙnq​(ℝ<0)p\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{<0}),\ r\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})\ \Rightarrow\ p\boxtimes_{n,q}r\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{<0}).

The qq-multiplicative convolution also preserves zero interlacing:

Proposition 3.5 (Preservation of interlacing, [Lam16, Theorems 29 and 30]).

Let p,p~,r∈ℙn∗​(ℝ)p,\widetilde{p},r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{*}(\mathbb{R}). If r∈ℙnq¯​(ℝ<0)r\in\overline{\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}}(\mathbb{R}_{<0}), p∈ℙnq¯​(ℝ)p\in\overline{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q}}(\mathbb{R}), p~∈ℙn​(ℝ)\widetilde{p}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}) and p≼p~p\preccurlyeq\widetilde{p}, then

p~⊠n,qr≼p⊠n,qr.\widetilde{p}\boxtimes_{n,q}r\preccurlyeq p\boxtimes_{n,q}r.
Remark 3.6.

Noticing that p≼rp\preccurlyeq r if and only if r⁡(−x)≼p⁡(−x)r(-x)\preccurlyeq p(-x) and that p⁡(x)⊠n,qr⁡(−x)=[p⊠n,qr]​(−x)p(x)\boxtimes_{n,q}r(-x)=[p\boxtimes_{n,q}r](-x), we can easily extend Proposition 3.5 to include polynomials with positive real roots. Namely, if p∈ℙnq¯​(ℝ)p\in\overline{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q}}(\mathbb{R}), p~∈ℙn​(ℝ)\widetilde{p}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}) and p≼p~p\preccurlyeq\widetilde{p}, then for a polynomial rr of degree nn,

r∈ℙnq¯​(ℝ>0)⇒p⊠n,qr≼p~⊠n,qr.r\in\overline{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q}}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})\quad\Rightarrow\quad p\boxtimes_{n,q}r\preccurlyeq\widetilde{p}\boxtimes_{n,q}r.

Let us now formulate two simple properties of the qq-multiplicative convolution.

Corollary 3.7.

If polynomials pp, rr satisfy p∈ℙnq1¯​(ℝ>0)p\in\overline{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q_{1}}}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}) and r∈ℙnq2¯​(ℝ>0)r\in\overline{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q_{2}}}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}), with q1≤q2<1q_{1}\leq q_{2}<1, then

p⊠n,q2r∈ℙnq1¯​(ℝ>0).p\boxtimes_{n,q_{2}}r\in\overline{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q_{1}}}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}).
Proof.

Let p∈ℙnq1¯​(ℝ>0)p\in\overline{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q_{1}}}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}) and r∈ℙnq2¯​(ℝ>0)r\in\overline{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q_{2}}}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}), then by (4), we have

p⁡(x)≼p⁡(q1​x)p(x)\preccurlyeq p(q_{1}x)

Taking the q2q_{2}-multiplicative convolution of p⁡(x)p(x) and p⁡(q1​x)p(q_{1}x) with r⁡(x)r(x) and using Proposition 3.5, we get

p⊠n,q2r⁡(x)≼p⁡(q1​x)⊠n,q2r⁡(x)=p⊠n,q2r⁡(q1​x),p\boxtimes_{n,q_{2}}r(x)\preccurlyeq p(q_{1}x)\boxtimes_{n,q_{2}}r(x)=p\boxtimes_{n,q_{2}}r(q_{1}x),

which is equivalent to

p⊠n,q2r∈ℙnq1¯​(ℝ>0).p\boxtimes_{n,q_{2}}r\in\overline{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q_{1}}}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}).

∎

Finally, one can check that qq-differentiation commutes with qq-multiplicative convolution up to a constant. This can be seen as a qq-multiplicative analog of [AFPU26, Remark 3.3].

Corollary 3.8.

The qq-multiplicative convolution satisfies that for p,r∈ℙnp,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n},

𝔡q​(p⊠n,qr)=(1−q−n)​𝔡q​(p)⊠n−1,q𝔡q​(r).\mathfrak{d}_{q}(p\boxtimes_{n,q}r)=\left(1-q^{-n}\right)\mathfrak{d}_{q}(p)\boxtimes_{n-1,q}\mathfrak{d}_{q}(r).
Proof.

Notice that for p∈ℙnp\in\mathbb{P}_{n} in the form (18), using (68) below, we get

𝔡q​p​(x)=∑i=0n−1(1−qn−i)​ei​(p)​xn−i−1,\mathfrak{d}_{q}p(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(1-q^{n-i})e_{i}(p)x^{n-i-1},

so that

ei(n−1)​(𝔡q​p)=(1−qi)​ei(n)​(p),e_{i}^{(n-1)}(\mathfrak{d}_{q}p)=(1-q^{i})e_{i}^{(n)}(p),

where the superscripts (n−1)(n-1) and (n)(n) are just to emphasize that the dependence of the degree in the coefficient notation (18). The conclusion now follows from the definition of ⊠n,q\boxtimes_{n,q}. ∎

3.2. Application to qq-hypergeometric polynomials

Our main contribution in Section 3 stems from the observation that the qq-multiplicative convolution of qq-hypergeometric polynomials preserves their character, and that the parameters of the resulting qq-hypergeometric polynomial are obtained by simple concatenation. This is the qq-analog of the result obtained in [MFMP24]:

Theorem 3.9.

Let 𝐚k∈ℝik\bm{a}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{i_{k}}, 𝐛k∈ℝjk\bm{b}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{j_{k}}, k=1,2k=1,2,

p1(x)=i1+1ϕj1(.q−n,𝒂1𝒃1.;q,x) and p2(x)=i2+1ϕj2(.q−n,𝒂2𝒃2.;q,x).p_{1}(x)={\ }_{i_{1}+1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{j_{1}}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n},\bm a_1}{\bm b_1};q,x\right)}\quad\text{ and }\quad p_{2}(x)={\ }_{i_{2}+1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{j_{2}}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n},\bm a_2}{\bm b_2};q,x\right)}.

Then

p1(x)⊠n,qp2(x)=i1+i2+1ϕj1+j2+1(.q−n,𝒂1,𝒂2𝒃1,𝒃2.;q,x)p_{1}(x)\boxtimes_{n,q}p_{2}(x)={\ }_{i_{1}+i_{2}+1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{j_{1}+j_{2}+1}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n},\bm a_1,\bm a_2}{\bm b_1,\bm b_2};q,x\right)}
Proof.

This is a straightforward computation: the kk-th coefficient of p1⊠n,qp2p_{1}\boxtimes_{n,q}p_{2} is

ek​(p1⊠n,qp2)\displaystyle e_{k}(p_{1}\boxtimes_{n,q}p_{2}) =(q,q)n−k(q−n,q)n−k​ek​(p1)​ek​(p2)\displaystyle=\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n-k}}{\left(q^{-n};q\right)_{n-k}}e_{k}(p_{1})e_{k}(p_{2})
=(−1)(j1+j2−i1−i2)​k​q(j1+j2−i1−i2)​(k2)​(q−n,q)k(q,q)k​(𝒂1,q)k​(𝒂2,q)k(𝒃1,q)k​(𝒃2,q)k\displaystyle=(-1)^{(j_{1}+j_{2}-i_{1}-i_{2})k}q^{(j_{1}+j_{2}-i_{1}-i_{2})\binom{k}{2}}\frac{\left(q^{-n};q\right)_{k}}{\left(q;q\right)_{k}}\frac{\left(\bm{a}_{1};q\right)_{k}\left(\bm{a}_{2};q\right)_{k}}{\left(\bm{b}_{1};q\right)_{k}\left(\bm{b}_{2};q\right)_{k}}

which coincides with the expression for the kk-th coefficient of

ϕj1+j2+1i1+i2+1​(.q−n,𝒂1,𝒂2𝒃1,𝒃2.,q,x).{\ }{}_{i_{1}+i_{2}+1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{j_{1}+j_{2}+1}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n},\bm a_1,\bm a_2}{\bm b_1,\bm b_2};q,x\right)}.

∎

As a direct consequence of Theorem 3.9 and the results of Section 2.3, we can construct qq-hypergeometric polynomials with real roots and logarithmic mesh ≤q\leq q (see Definition 2.3).

Example 3.13.

Multiple orthogonal polynomials (of type II) are polynomials satisfying orthogonality conditions with respect to m≥1m\geq 1 positive measures. 4. qq-Additive Convolution

In this section, we introduce a qq-analog of the finite free additive convolution.

4.1. Definition and properties

Definition 4.1.

Given two polynomials, pp and rr, of degree at most nn, the nn-th qq-additive finite free convolution of pp and rr, denoted as p⊞n,qrp\boxplus_{n,q}r, is a polynomial of degree at most nn, which, following the notational convention (18), is defined as

[p⊞n,qr](x):=∑k=0nek(p⊞n,qr)xn−k,[p\boxplus_{n,q}r](x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}e_{k}(p\boxplus_{n,q}r)\,x^{n-k},

with

(33) ek(p⊞n,qr)=(−1)k∑i+j=k(q,q)n−i​(q,q)n−j(q,q)n​(q,q)n−kei(p)ej(r).e_{k}(p\boxplus_{n,q}r)=(-1)^{k}\sum_{i+j=k}\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n-i}\left(q;q\right)_{n-j}}{\left(q;q\right)_{n}\left(q;q\right)_{n-k}}\,e_{i}(p)e_{j}(r).

The qq-additive finite free convolution exhibits several convenient properties. It is a commutative and associative linear operator from ℙn×ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n}\times\mathbb{P}_{n} to ℙn\mathbb{P}_{n}: if p,r,g∈ℙnp,r,g\in\mathbb{P}_{n}, and α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}, then

(αp+g)⊞n,qr=α(p⊞n,qr)+g⊞n,qr.(\alpha p+g)\boxplus_{n,q}r=\alpha(p\boxplus_{n,q}r)+g\boxplus_{n,q}r.

Moreover, it is compatible with the dilation: for α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R},

p(αx)⊞n,qr(αx)=[p⊞n,qr](αx).p(\alpha x)\boxplus_{n,q}r(\alpha x)=[p\boxplus_{n,q}r](\alpha x).

Furthermore, xnx^{n} is the identity element for ⊞n,q\boxplus_{n,q}:

(34) p⊞n,qxn\displaystyle p\boxplus_{n,q}x^{n} =p for all ​p∈ℙn.\displaystyle=p\qquad\text{ for all }p\in\mathbb{P}_{n}.
Remark 4.2 (Relation with additive finite free convolution).

Recall that for polynomials p,r∈ℙnp,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n} in the form (18), its nn-th additive finite free convolution is

(35) [p⊞nr](x):=∑k=0nxn−k(−1)k∑i+j=k(n−i)!​(n−j)!n!​(n−k)!ei(p)ej(r).[p\boxplus_{n}r](x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}x^{n-k}(-1)^{k}\sum_{i+j=k}\frac{(n-i)!(n-j)!}{n!(n-k)!}\,e_{i}(p)e_{j}(r).

Notice that this is the limit of the qq-additive convolution when qq tends to 1:

limq→1p⊞n,qr=p⊞nr.\lim_{q\to 1}p\boxplus_{n,q}r=p\boxplus_{n}r.

Indeed, the limit can be checked coefficient-wise using property (6),

limq→1(q,q)n−i​(q,q)n−j(q,q)n​(q,q)n−k=(n−i)!​(n−j)!n!​(n−k)!.\lim_{q\to 1}\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n-i}\left(q;q\right)_{n-j}}{\left(q;q\right)_{n}\left(q;q\right)_{n-k}}=\frac{(n-i)!(n-j)!}{n!(n-k)!}.

It turns out that this convolution also can be computed in terms of qq-differential operators defined in (16), which can be taken as an alternative definition. With a polynomial p∈ℙnp\in\mathbb{P}_{n} we can associate its unique (𝔡q)(\mathfrak{d}_{q})-dual polynomial p^∈ℙn\widehat{p}\in\mathbb{P}_{n} such that

p^​(𝔡q)​[xn]=p⁡(x).\widehat{p}(\mathfrak{d}_{q})[x^{n}]=p(x).

This correspondence can be made explicit: for

p⁡(x)=∑j=0nej​(p)​xn−j,p(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}e_{j}(p)x^{n-j},

we have

(36) p^​(x)=∑k=0n(−1)k​q(k2)−n​k(q−n,q)k​ek​(p)​xk.\widehat{p}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^{k}\frac{q^{\binom{k}{2}-nk}}{\left(q^{-n};q\right)_{k}}e_{k}(p)x^{k}.
Proposition 4.3.

Given polynomials p,r∈ℙnp,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}, let p^\widehat{p} and r^\widehat{r} be their (𝔡q)(\mathfrak{d}_{q})-duals. Then,

(37) [p⊞n,qr](x)\displaystyle[p\boxplus_{n,q}r](x) =p^​(𝔡q)​r^​(𝔡q)​[xn].\displaystyle=\widehat{p}(\mathfrak{d}_{q})\widehat{r}(\mathfrak{d}_{q})[x^{n}].
Proof.

The conclusion follows from a straightforward computation and formula (36):

p^​(𝔡q)​r^​(𝔡q)​[xn]\displaystyle\widehat{p}(\mathfrak{d}_{q})\widehat{r}(\mathfrak{d}_{q})[x^{n}] =p^​(𝔡q)​r​(x)=∑j=0n∑i=0n(q,q)n−i(q,q)n​ej​(r)​ei​(p)​𝔡qi​xn−j\displaystyle=\widehat{p}(\mathfrak{d}_{q})r(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n-i}}{\left(q;q\right)_{n}}e_{j}(r)e_{i}(p)\mathfrak{d}_{q}^{i}x^{n-j}
=∑j=0n∑i=0n(q,q)n−i​(q,q)n−j(q,q)n​(q,q)n−j−iej(r)ei(p)xn−j−i=p⊞n,qr(x).\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n-i}\left(q;q\right)_{n-j}}{\left(q;q\right)_{n}\left(q;q\right)_{n-j-i}}e_{j}(r)e_{i}(p)x^{n-j-i}=p\boxplus_{n,q}r(x).

∎

4.2. Preservation of real roots

One of the convenient features of ⊞n\boxplus_{n} is that it preserves real roots. Unfortunately, ⊞n,q\boxplus_{n,q} does not share this property, in general.

Example 4.4.

Let

p⁡(x)=x2−0.80​x+0.12∈ℙ20.5​(ℝ>0), and ​r​(x)=x2−0.75​x+0.09∈ℙ20.5​(ℝ>0).p(x)=x^{2}-0.80x+0.12\in\mathbb{P}^{0.5}_{2}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}),\text{ and }r(x)=x^{2}-0.75x+0.09\in\mathbb{P}^{0.5}_{2}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}).

Nevertheless,

(p⊞2,0.5r)(x)=x2−1.55x+0.61,(p\boxplus_{2,0.5}r)(x)=x^{2}-1.55x+0.61,

which has complex roots.

However, a simple modification of ⊞n,q\boxplus_{n,q} allows us to restore the real roots preservation for polynomials with lmesh <q<q. Specifically, it turns out that

p,r∈ℙnq(ℝ)⇒1ϕ1(.q−n0.;q,−x)⊠n,q(p⊞n,qr)∈ℙn(ℝ).p,r\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R})\quad\Rightarrow\quad{\ }_{1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{1}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n}}{0};q,-x\right)}\boxtimes_{n,q}\left(p\boxplus_{n,q}r\right)\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}).

We prove this fact in two steps. First, we establish a useful identity combining all four finite free convolutions (⊠n\boxtimes_{n}, ⊠n,q\boxtimes_{n,q}, ⊞n\boxplus_{n}, and ⊞n,q\boxplus_{n,q}), which allows us to reduce the claimed result to the known real-roots preservation properties of ⊞n\boxplus_{n}, ⊠n\boxtimes_{n}, and ⊠n,q\boxtimes_{n,q}. This is a purely algebraic result of independent interest that does not make any assumption on the location of the roots:

Proposition 4.5.

For any polynomials p,r∈ℙnp,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n},

(38) ϕ11(.q−n0.;q,−x)⊠n,q(p⊞n,qr){\ }{}_{1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{1}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n}}{0};q,-x\right)}\boxtimes_{n,q}\left(p\boxplus_{n,q}r\right) =[(Un⊠n,qp)⊞n(Un⊠n,qr)]⊠nVn,\displaystyle=[(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}p)\boxplus_{n}(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r)]\boxtimes_{n}V_{n},

where

(39) Un(x):=∑k=0n(q−n,q)kk!xk, and Vn(x):=∑k=0n(−n)k¯(q,q)kq(k2)xk.U_{n}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{\left(q^{-n};q\right)_{k}}{k!}x^{k},\quad\text{ and }\quad V_{n}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{\left(-n\right)^{\overline{k}}}{\left(q;q\right)_{k}}q^{\binom{k}{2}}x^{k}.
Remark 4.6.

It is easy to check that (38) is equivalent to the identity

p⊞n,qr=[(Un⊠n,qp)⊞n(Un⊠n,qr)]⊠nV^n,p\boxplus_{n,q}r=[(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}p)\boxplus_{n}(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r)]\boxtimes_{n}\widehat{V}_{n},

where

V^n​(x):=∑k=0n(−n)k¯(q,q)k​xk.\widehat{V}_{n}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{\left(-n\right)^{\overline{k}}}{\left(q;q\right)_{k}}x^{k}.
Proof.

We show that the corresponding coefficients of each side of (38) match. As agreed, we use the notation for the coefficients as in (18).

By the definition of qq-multiplicative convolution (19),

ej​(Un⊠n,qp)=(q,q)n−j(n−j)!​ej​(p)and ej​(Un⊠n,qr)=(q,q)n−j(n−j)!​ej​(r).e_{j}(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}p)=\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n-j}}{(n-j)!}e_{j}(p)\quad\text{and }\quad e_{j}(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r)=\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n-j}}{(n-j)!}e_{j}(r).

Therefore, by the definition (35), for k∈{0,1,…,n}k\in\{0,1,\dots,n\},

ek((Un⊠n,qp)⊞n(Un⊠n,qr))=∑i+j=k(q,q)n−i​(q,q)n−jn!​(n−k)!ej(p)ei(r).e_{k}((U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}p)\boxplus_{n}(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r))=\sum_{i+j=k}\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n-i}\left(q;q\right)_{n-j}}{n!(n-k)!}\,e_{j}(p)e_{i}(r).

The conclusion follows from the formula for the multiplicative convolution (24)

ek([(Un⊠n,qp)⊞n(Un⊠n,qr)]⊠nVn)\displaystyle e_{k}([(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}p)\boxplus_{n}(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r)]\boxtimes_{n}V_{n}) =∑i+j=k(q,q)n−i​(q,q)n−jn!​(q,q)n−k​ej​(p)​ei​(r)\displaystyle=\sum_{i+j=k}\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n-i}\left(q;q\right)_{n-j}}{n!\left(q;q\right)_{n-k}}\,e_{j}(p)e_{i}(r)
=(q,q)nn!ek(p⊞n,qr).\displaystyle=\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n}}{n!}e_{k}(p\boxplus_{n,q}r).

∎

For our second step, we need the preservation properties of real roots for the remaining convolutions appearing in the identity (38). We collected and summarized next the classical results of Szegő [Sze22] and Walsh [Wal22], see also [MFMP24]: for p,g,r∈ℙnp,g,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n},

(40) p≺g,r∈ℙn​(ℝ)\displaystyle p\prec g,\ r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}) ⇒p⊞nr≺g⊞nr\displaystyle\ \Rightarrow\ p\boxplus_{n}r\prec g\boxplus_{n}r
(41) p,r∈ℙn​(ℝ)\displaystyle p,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}) ⇒p⊞nr∈ℙn(ℝ),\displaystyle\ \Rightarrow\ p\boxplus_{n}r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}),
(42) p,r∈ℙn​(ℝ>0)\displaystyle p,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}) ⇒p⊞nr∈ℙn(ℝ>0),\displaystyle\ \Rightarrow\ p\boxplus_{n}r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}),
(43) p∈ℙn​(ℝ),r∈ℙn​(ℝ>0)\displaystyle p\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}),\ r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}) ⇒p⊠nr∈ℙn​(ℝ),\displaystyle\ \Rightarrow\ p\boxtimes_{n}r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}),
(44) p,r∈ℙn​(ℝ>0)\displaystyle p,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}) ⇒p⊠nr∈ℙn​(ℝ>0),\displaystyle\ \Rightarrow\ p\boxtimes_{n}r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}),
(45) p≺g,r∈ℙn​(ℝ>0)\displaystyle p\prec g,\ r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}) ⇒p⊠nr≺g⊠nr.\displaystyle\ \Rightarrow\ p\boxtimes_{n}r\prec g\boxtimes_{n}r.

Additionally, we will need the result from [KSV11] that multiplicative convolution preserves the smallest lmesh: given q<1q<1 and polynomials pp, rr such that p∈ℙnq¯​(ℝ>0)p\in\overline{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q}}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}) and r∈ℙn¯​(ℝ>0)r\in\overline{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}), it holds that

p⊠nr∈ℙnq¯​(ℝ>0).p\boxtimes_{n}r\in\overline{\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q}}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}).

The last ingredient is the following lemma, whose proof is deferred to Appendix A.

Lemma 4.7.

For every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, both polynomials (39) are in ℙnq​(ℝ>0)\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}).

We are now ready to state and prove the main result of this section, partially announced before:

Theorem 4.8 (Preservation of real roots).

Let p,r∈ℙnp,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}. Then

  1. (i)

    p,r∈ℙnq(ℝ)⇒1ϕ1(.q−n0.;q,−x)⊠n,q(p⊞n,qr)∈ℙn(ℝ)p,r\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R})\ \Rightarrow\ {\ }_{1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{1}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n}}{0};q,-x\right)}\boxtimes_{n,q}\left(p\boxplus_{n,q}r\right)\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}).

  2. (ii)

    p,r∈ℙnq(ℝ>0)⇒1ϕ1(.q−n0.;q,−x)⊠n,q(p⊞n,qr)∈ℙnq(ℝ>0)p,r\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})\ \Rightarrow\ {\ }_{1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{1}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n}}{0};q,-x\right)}\boxtimes_{n,q}\left(p\boxplus_{n,q}r\right)\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}).

Notice that in (i) we can only claim that the resulting polynomials are real-rooted; no bound on the lmesh is established.

Proof.

We will only show (i), being the proof of the other statement similar. By assumption, p,r∈ℙnq​(ℝ)p,r\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}), while Lemma 4.7 asserts that Un,Vn∈ℙnq​(ℝ>0)U_{n},V_{n}\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}). From Proposition 3.4 we get that

Un⊠n,qp∈ℙnq​(ℝ)andUn⊠n,qr∈ℙnq​(ℝ).U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}p\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R})\qquad\text{and}\qquad U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}).

Property (41) then yields that

[(Un⊠n,qp)⊞n(Un⊠n,qr)]∈ℙn(ℝ).[(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}p)\boxplus_{n}(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r)]\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}).

Finally, since Vn∈ℙnq​(ℝ>0)V_{n}\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}), (43) implies that

[(Un⊠n,qp)⊞n(Un⊠n,qr)]⊠nVn∈ℙnq(ℝ).[(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}p)\boxplus_{n}(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r)]\boxtimes_{n}V_{n}\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}).

The conclusion follows from the identity (38). ∎

The same ideas yield an interlacing-preservation result for the corrected qq-additive convolution.

Theorem 4.9 (Preservation of interlacing).

Let g∈ℙn​(ℝ)g\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}) and p,r∈ℙnq​(ℝ)p,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q}(\mathbb{R}) such that p≺gp\prec g. Then

(46) ϕ11(.q−n0.;q,−x)⊠n,q(p⊞n,qr)≺1ϕ1(.q−n0.;q,−x)⊠n,q(g⊞n,qr){\ }{}_{1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{1}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n}}{0};q,-x\right)}\boxtimes_{n,q}\left(p\boxplus_{n,q}r\right)\prec{\ }_{1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{1}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n}}{0};q,-x\right)}\boxtimes_{n,q}\left(g\boxplus_{n,q}r\right)
Proof.

Since UnU_{n} belongs to ℙnq​(ℝ>0)\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}) (see Lemma 4.7), we get the following facts

Un⊠n,qp≺Un⊠n,qg\displaystyle U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}p\prec U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}g  (by Proposition 3.5),\displaystyle\quad\text{ (by Proposition \ref{lem:preservinginterlacingMult})},
Un⊠n,qr∈ℙnq​(ℝ)\displaystyle U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q}(\mathbb{R}) (by Proposition 3.4).\displaystyle\quad\text{(by Proposition \ref{prop:realrootedness})}.

Using those facts and (40), we get

(Un⊠n,qp)⊞n(Un⊠n,qr)≺(Un⊠n,qg)⊞n(Un⊠n,qr).(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}p)\boxplus_{n}(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r)\prec(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}g)\boxplus_{n}(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r).

Finally, since VnV_{n} has positive roots, equation (45) yields

[(Un⊠n,qp)⊞n(Un⊠n,qr)]⊠nVn≺[(Un⊞n,qg)⊞n(Un⊠n,qr)]⊠nVn.[(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}p)\boxplus_{n}(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r)]\boxtimes_{n}V_{n}\prec[(U_{n}\boxplus_{n,q}g)\boxplus_{n}(U_{n}\boxtimes_{n,q}r)]\boxtimes_{n}V_{n}.

The conclusion follows from the identity (38), Proposition 3.5, and line 9 of Table 1. ∎

To finish this section, let us mention another interesting case in which ⊞n,q\boxplus_{n,q} preserves the real roots. The result follows from inductively using the fact that for α>0\alpha>0 the operator 𝔡q−α\mathfrak{d}_{q}-\alpha preserves the qq-lmesh. Namely, if p∈ℙnq​(ℝ)p\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}), then (𝔡q−α)​p∈ℙnq​(ℝ)(\mathfrak{d}_{q}-\alpha)p\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}).

Theorem 4.10.

If r⁡(x)=r^​(𝔡q)​[xn]r(x)=\widehat{r}(\mathfrak{d}_{q})[x^{n}], where r^∈ℙn​(ℝ>0)\widehat{r}\in\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}), and p∈ℙnq​(ℝ>0)p\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}) then p⊞n,qr∈ℙnq(ℝ>0)p\boxplus_{n,q}r\in\mathbb{P}_{n}^{q}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}).

Proof.

This is just a reformulation of [Fis08, Corollary 8.69 part 6] after using the interpretation of ⊞n,q\boxplus_{n,q} in terms of 𝔡q\mathfrak{d}_{q} given in Proposition 4.3. ∎

5. qq-additive convolution of qq-hypergeometric polynomials

In this section, we illustrate the application of the qq-additive convolution to qq-hypergeometric polynomials. The main tool will be the expression for ⊞n,q\boxplus_{n,q} in terms of qq-differential operators obtained in Proposition 4.3. We provide a general method to translate product identities of qq-hypergeometric functions into convolutional identities for qq-hypergeometric polynomials. This is a qq-analog of the results from [MFMP24] in the hypergeometric setting.

Our approach relies on the notion of duality, discussed above, i.e., formulas of the form

f⁡(𝔡q)​[xn]=p⁡(x),f(\mathfrak{d}_{q})[x^{n}]=p(x),

where 𝔡q\mathfrak{d}_{q} was defined in (16), ff is a qq-hypergeometric function, and pp is a qq-hypergeometric polynomial. A basic example of such a formula is

(47) rϕs(.𝒂𝒃.;q,𝔡q)[xn]∝r′ϕs′(.q−n,𝒃′𝒂′.;q,x).{\ }_{r}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{s}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\bm a}{\bm b};q,\mathfrak{d}_{q}\right)}[x^{n}]\propto{\ }_{r^{\prime}}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{s^{\prime}}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n},\bm b'}{\bm a'};q,x\right)}.

We will explain how 𝒂\bm{a}, 𝒃\bm{b} are explicitly related to 𝒂′\bm{a}^{\prime}, 𝒃′\bm{b}^{\prime}. We further provide variations of this formula in which the right-hand side is evaluated at c​xcx or x2x^{2} (instead of xx), or in which we use 𝔡q2\mathfrak{d}_{q}^{2} or 𝔡q2\mathfrak{d}_{q^{2}} on the left-hand side.

Once we have explicitly computed such formulas, the procedure is as follows: starting with a product identity of qq-hypergeometric functions,

f1​(x)​f2​(x)=f3​(x),f_{1}(x)f_{2}(x)=f_{3}(x),

we formally evaluate it at 𝔡q\mathfrak{d}_{q} and use Proposition 4.3, to arrive at identities of the form

p1⊞n,qp2=p3,p_{1}\boxplus_{n,q}p_{2}=p_{3},

where pi​(x):=fi​(𝔡q)​[xn]p_{i}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=f_{i}(\mathfrak{d}_{q})[x^{n}] for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3.

We will study three relevant cases and provide examples of how to use this method for specific polynomials.

5.1. From qq-hypergeometric differential operators to qq-hypergeometric polynomials

We begin by providing precise formulas of the form (47) connecting qq-hypergeometric polynomials and qq-hypergeometric functions in 𝔡q\mathfrak{d}_{q}. The proof of these formulas is rather technical and is presented in Appendix B.

Lemma 5.1.

Let 𝐚=(a1,…,ar)∈ℝr\bm{a}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{r})\in\mathbb{R}^{r} and 𝐛=(b1,…,bs)∈ℝs\bm{b}=(b_{1},\dots,b_{s})\in\mathbb{R}^{s} be tuples of non-zero numbers satisfying restrictions (9). For c≠0c\neq 0, define the corresponding constant

(48) c′:=b1​b2​…​bsc​a1​a2​…​ar.c^{\prime}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{b_{1}b_{2}\dots b_{s}}{ca_{1}a_{2}\dots a_{r}}.

Then the following identities hold:

(49) ϕsr​(.𝒂𝒃.,q,c​𝔡q)​[xn]{\ }{}_{r}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{s}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\bm a}{\bm b};q,c\mathfrak{d}_{q}\right)}[x^{n}] ∝r+s+1ϕr+s(.q−n,𝒃−1​q1−n,𝟎r𝒂−1​q1−n,𝟎s.;q,c′qx),\displaystyle\propto{\ }_{r+s+1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{r+s}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n},\bm b^{-1} q^{1-n},\bm 0_{r}}{\bm a^{-1} q^{1-n}, \bm 0_{s}};q,c^{\prime}qx\right)},
(50) ϕsr​(.𝒂𝒃.,q,c​𝔡q2)​[xn]{\ }{}_{r}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{s}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\bm a }{\bm b};q,c\mathfrak{d}_{q^{2}}\right)}[x^{n}] ∝r+s+2ϕr+s+1(.q−n,𝒃−1​q1−n,𝟎r+1𝒂−1​q1−n,−q,𝟎s.;q,c′qx),and\displaystyle\propto{\ }_{r+s+2}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{r+s+1}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n},\bm b^{-1} q^{1-n},\bm 0_{r+1}}{\bm a^{-1} q^{1-n},-q, \bm 0_{s}};q,c^{\prime}qx\right)},\qquad\text{and}
(51) ϕsr​(.𝒂𝒃.,q2,c​𝔡q2)​[x2​n]{\ }{}_{r}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{s}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\bm a }{\bm b};q^{2},c\mathfrak{d}_{q}^{2}\right)}[x^{2n}] ∝r+s+2ϕr+s+1(.q−2​n,𝒃−1​q2−2​n,𝟎r+1𝒂−1​q2−2​n,q,𝟎s.;q2,c′q2x2),\displaystyle\propto{\ }_{r+s+2}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{r+s+1}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-2n},\bm b^{-1} q^{2-2n},\bm 0_{r+1}}{\bm a^{-1} q^{2-2n},q, \bm 0_{s}};q^{2},c^{\prime}q^{2}x^{2}\right)},

where 𝟎r\bm{0}_{r} and 𝟎s\bm{0}_{s} stand for tuples of rr and ss zeros, respectively.

Remark 5.2.

The formulas above may simplify due to cancellations of the zero tuples in the upper and lower sets of parameters. For instance, in (49), if r=sr=s then both zero tuples cancel each other. Otherwise, a single zero tuple of length |r−s||r-s| will appear in the upper (if r>sr>s) or lower (if r<sr<s) set of parameters. A similar analysis is valid for (50) and (51).

Furthermore, the restriction that a1,…,ar,b1,…,bs≠0a_{1},\dots,a_{r},b_{1},\dots,b_{s}\neq 0 can be weakened. A more general version of the statement appears as Lemma B.1. It can be derived as a limit case of Lemma 5.1, by letting a parameter tend to zero. For instance, if ai→0a_{i}\to 0, then ai−1​q1−n→∞a_{i}^{-1}q^{1-n}\to\infty, and the corresponding parameter on the right-hand side of (49) disappears at the cost of scaling the polynomial by q1−nq^{1-n}. A similar reasoning works for (50) and (51).

In the rest of the section, we derive qq-additive convolution formulas from the identities (49)–(51). Instead of being exhaustive, we focus on the three most common types of product formulas.

5.2. Formulas with ⊞n,q\boxplus_{n,q}

We begin with the simplest product formula involving only standard qq-hypergeometric polynomials.

Let 𝐚k∈ℝrk\bm{a}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{k}}, 𝐛k∈ℝsk\bm{b}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{s_{k}}, k=1,2,3k=1,2,3, with non-zero entries satisfying restrictions (9). p2(x):=r2+s2+1ϕr2+s2(.q−n,𝒃2−1​q1−n, 0r2𝒂2−1​q1−n, 0s2.;q,c2′qx)p_{2}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}={\ }_{r_{2}+s_{2}+1}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{r_{2}+s_{2}}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{q^{-n}\, ,\, \bm b_2^{-1} q^{1-n}\, ,\, \bm 0_{r_2}}{\bm a_2^{-1} q^{1-n}\, ,\, \bm 0_{s_2}};q,c_{2}^{\prime}qx\right)}

We formally replace the variable xx by 𝔡q\mathfrak{d}_{q} in (52) and apply the resulting qq-differential operator to xnx^{n}:

ϕs1r1(.𝒂1𝒃1.;q,c1𝔡q)r2ϕs2(.𝒂2𝒃2.;q,c2𝔡q)[xn]=r3ϕs3(.𝒂3𝒃3.;q,c3𝔡q)[xn].{\ }{}_{r_{1}}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{s_{1}}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\bm a_1}{\bm b_1};q,c_{1}\mathfrak{d}_{q}\right)}{\ }_{r_{2}}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{s_{2}}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\bm a_2 }{\bm b_2};q,c_{2}\mathfrak{d}_{q}\right)}[x^{n}]={\ }_{r_{3}}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{s_{3}}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\bm a_3}{\bm b_3};q,c_{3}\mathfrak{d}_{q}\right)}[x^{n}].

Given nonzero constants c1,c2,c3c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}, define the corresponding constants c1′,c2′,c3′c^{\prime}_{1},c^{\prime}_{2},c^{\prime}_{3} in terms of the parameters as in (48).

ϕs1r1(.𝒂1𝒃1.;q,c1𝔡q)r2ϕs2(.𝒂2𝒃2.;q,c2𝔡q)[x2​n]=r3ϕs3(.𝒂3𝒃3.;q2,c3𝔡q2)[x2​n].{\ }{}_{r_{1}}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{s_{1}}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\bm a_1}{\bm b_1};q,c_{1}\mathfrak{d}_{q}\right)}{\ }_{r_{2}}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{s_{2}}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\bm a_2}{\bm b_2};q,c_{2}\mathfrak{d}_{q}\right)}[x^{2n}]={\ }_{r_{3}}{\mathcal{\phi}}_{s_{3}}{\left(\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{\bm a_3}{\bm b_3};q^{2},c_{3}\mathfrak{d}_{q}^{2}\right)}[x^{2n}].

We now apply this result to the case where c1=1c_{1}=1 and c2=−1c_{2}=-1. Notice that these examples can be seen as a qq-analog of symmetrization of polynomials as studied in [CMP25, Sections 3.2 and 4.2]. This notion can be defined for any polynomial:

Notation 5.7.

The qq-symmetrization of p∈ℙnp\in\mathbb{P}_{n} is the polynomial

(57) qSym(p):=p⊞n,q(Dil−1p),\mathrm{qSym}\left(p\right)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=p\boxplus_{n,q}\left(\text{Dil}_{-1}p\right)\text{,}

where (Dil−1​p)​(x):=(−1)n​p​(−x)(\text{Dil}_{-1}p)(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=(-1)^{n}p(-x).

From (33) it is readily seen that the polynomials qSym⁡(p)\mathrm{qSym}\left(p\right) are even (their odd coefficients vanish). Further properties of symmetrization are straightforward (see also [CMP25, Sections 3.2]): for p,r∈ℙnp,r\in\mathbb{P}_{n},

  1. (1)

    qSym⁡(p)=qSym⁡(Dil−1​p)\mathrm{qSym}\left(p\right)=\mathrm{qSym}\left(\text{Dil}_{-1}p\right);

  2. (2)

    If pp is an even polynomial, then qSym(p)=p⊞n,qp\mathrm{qSym}\left(p\right)=p\boxplus_{n,q}p;

  3. (3)

    qSym(p⊞n,qr)=qSym(p)⊞n,qqSym(r)\mathrm{qSym}\left(p\boxplus_{n,q}r\right)=\mathrm{qSym}\left(p\right)\boxplus_{n,q}\mathrm{qSym}\left(r\right);

  4. (4)

    qSym⁡(Dilα​p)=Dilα​qSym​(p)\mathrm{qSym}\left(\text{Dil}_{\alpha}p\right)=\text{Dil}_{\alpha}\mathrm{qSym}\left(p\right).

Appendix A Polynomials with real roots.

Here we will prove both claims of Lemma 4.7:

Un(x):=∑k=0n(q−n,q)kk!xk∈ℙnq(ℝ>0) and Vn(x):=∑k=0n(−n)k¯(q,q)kq(k2)xk∈ℙnq(ℝ>0).U_{n}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{\left(q^{-n};q\right)_{k}}{k!}x^{k}\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0})\quad\text{ and }\quad V_{n}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{\left(-n\right)^{\overline{k}}}{\left(q;q\right)_{k}}q^{\binom{k}{2}}x^{k}\in\mathbb{P}^{q}_{n}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}).

We prove our assertions by induction on the degree nn.

Now, for n=2n=2 we notice that

with 0<λ1​(U2)<λ2​(U2)0<\lambda_{1}(U_{2})<\lambda_{2}(U_{2}). Thus, its logarithmic root separation is

Appendix B Proof of technical lemmas

The goal of this section is to prove Lemma 5.1. Although it requires lengthy and cumbersome computations, the proof is, in a certain sense, straightforward once one understands the effect of applying the operators 𝔡q\mathfrak{d}_{q}, 𝔡q2\mathfrak{d}_{q^{2}}, and 𝔡q2\mathfrak{d}^{2}_{q} to powers of xx.

Recall that for q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1), our (modified) qq-derivative operator 𝔡q\mathfrak{d}_{q} is defined as

𝔡q​f​(x):={f⁡(x)−f⁡(q​x)x,x≠0f′​(0),x=0.\mathfrak{d}_{q}f(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\begin{cases}\frac{f(x)-f(qx)}{x},&x\neq 0\\ f^{\prime}(0),&x=0.\end{cases}

It is readily seen that 𝔡q\mathfrak{d}_{q} is linear. When applied to powers of xx it yields, for n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, that

(68) 𝔡q​xn=(1−qn)​xn−1and𝔡q​1=0.\mathfrak{d}_{q}x^{n}=(1-q^{n})x^{n-1}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathfrak{d}_{q}1=0.

Thus, qq-differentiating kk times gives

(69) 𝔡qk​[xn]=xn−k​∏i=0k−1(1−qn−i)=xn−k​(−1)k​qn​k−(k2)=(q,q)n(q,q)n−k​xn−k.\mathfrak{d}_{q}^{k}[x^{n}]=x^{n-k}\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(1-q^{n-i})=x^{n-k}(-1)^{k}q^{nk-\binom{k}{2}}=\frac{\left(q;q\right)_{n}}{\left(q;q\right)_{n-k}}x^{n-k}.

We can use this formula to check that repeatedly applying 𝔡q2\mathfrak{d}_{q^{2}} is related to repeatedly applying 𝔡q\mathfrak{d}_{q}:

(70) 𝔡q2k​[xn]=xn−k​∏i=0k−1(1−qn−i)​(1+qn−i)=qn​k−(k2)​(−q−n,q)k​𝔡qk​[xn].\mathfrak{d}_{q^{2}}^{k}[x^{n}]=x^{n-k}\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(1-q^{n-i})(1+q^{n-i})=q^{nk-\binom{k}{2}}\left(-q^{-n};q\right)_{k}\mathfrak{d}^{k}_{q}[x^{n}].

Similarly we notice that applying 𝔡q2\mathfrak{d}_{q}^{2} repeatedly is related to 𝔡q2\mathfrak{d}_{q^{2}}. Specifically,

(71) 𝔡q2​k​[x2​n]=(−1)k​q2​n​k−2​(k2)−k​(q−2​n+1,q2)k​𝔡q2k​[tn]|t=x2.\mathfrak{d}_{q}^{2k}[x^{2n}]=(-1)^{k}q^{2nk-2\binom{k}{2}-k}\left(q^{-2n+1};q^{2}\right)_{k}\mathfrak{d}^{k}_{q^{2}}[t^{n}]\bigg|_{t=x^{2}}.

The last technical bit that we require is the following formula, a direct consequence of the definition of the qq-factorials (5),

(72) (a,q)k​(−1)k​q−(k2)=(−1)n​q−(n2)​(a,q)nan−k​(a−1​q1−n,q)n−k.\left(a;q\right)_{k}(-1)^{k}q^{-\binom{k}{2}}=\frac{(-1)^{n}q^{-\binom{n}{2}}\left(a;q\right)_{n}}{a^{n-k}\left(a^{-1}q^{1-n};q\right)_{n-k}}.

Remark B.2.

Notice that on the left-hand side of (49) the vectors of zeros 𝟎i\bm{0}_{i} and 𝟎j\bm{0}_{j} may cancel each other. In practice, we need to consider the case when at least one of ii and jj is 0. The same goes for the right-hand side with rr and ss. The reason we opted to include both vectors is to provide a unified treatment and avoid distinguishing four different cases in which the zeros might be above or below on each side of the equation.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
